newsitem.title: INDIA: Commodities - Pepper, coffee enliven Indian markets.
newsitem.headline: Commodities - Pepper, coffee enliven Indian markets.

text.p: Pepper added spice to otherwise insipid trade in Indian commodities in the week to Saturday, marked by a mild concern over a delay in the arrival of the monsoon, traders said on Sunday.
"The pepper market is very firm because of a global shortage of supplies," said T. Vidyasagar, president of the Indian Pepper and Spices Trade Association (IPSTA).
Vidyasagar said he would expect domestic prices to rise to 150 rupees per kg in the next week from 135 rupees at present.
"Indian exports are brisk, because India is the only supplier of pepper at present," he said. Indonesian and Malaysian crops are expected after July and August, he said.
"Our stocks are also dwindling and I expect pepper prices to firm further," Vidyasagar said.
Coffee promises to provide a heady brew as prices moved sharply.
"Coffee prices are volatile globally and are affecting domestic trends too," said Arun Bidappa, chief ececutive of Karnataka Coffee Brokers Pvt Ltd.
He said coffee prices were quoted around 197 cents per pound now after falling sharply from a 20-year high of 318 cents per pound towards the end of May.
"Now there are fears of a frost in Brazil, a major coffee producer, which might move prices," Bidappa said.
Indian coffee retail prices have also risen sharply in the last month to 220 rupees per kg from 160 rupees per kg.
"Prices will be firm in the current week," Bidappa said.
Price movements in other agricultural commodities have been slow despite some concern about a week's delay in the arrival of monsoon rains in India.

"A delay of about a week in the arrival of monsoon had caused some concern. But now that the monsoon has arrived, it is expected to make up for the delay," said Bombay Oilseeds and Oils Exchange president Navin Shah.
"The monsoon delay has no impact on edible oil prices. I expect them to move narrowly during the next week," Shah said.
India, predominently agricultural, depends on the four-month June-September monsoon rains for growth of its crops.
Groundnut oil fell eight rupees to 355 and imported palmolein lost a rupee to 269 in the week to Saturday.
Shah said India's liberal market policy of allowing free imports of edible oils had stabilised supplies and prices.
He said Indian traders imported 100,000 tonnes of palmolein in May and booked around 80,000 tonnes for both June and July.
In the central Indian state of Madhya Pradesh, farmers are getting ready for sowing soybean in the last week of June.
The state accounts for nearly 75 percent of India's total soybean production, estimated in 1996/97 (November/October) at 3.7 million tonnes, down from the previous year's 4.2 million.
"Farmers are awaiting rains. Pre-monsoon showers had already begun," said Davesh Jain, president of the Soybean Porcessors' Association of India (SOPA).
Jain said the area under soybean cultivation was expected to rise to nearly 5.0 million hectares in the 1997/98 season from 4.5 million in the previous year.
In the week to Saturday, soybean prices ruled steady at 12,400/12,900 rupees per tonne.
Gold failed to provide glitter, moving tardily in a market devoid of demand following the end of the wedding season in May.
"Bullion prices will remain weak, unless provoked by some sharp movement in world markets," said M.L. Damani, president of the Bombay Bullion Association.
In the week to Saturday, gold prices fell 50 rupees per 10 grammes to 4,630 rupees. Silver slumped 180 rupees to 4,715 rupees per kg in the same period.
Damani said business volumes fell to about 400 kg in silver and 25 kg in gold from 1,600 kg and 100 kg respectively in May.
Some activity is expected in non-ferrous metals, especially copper, in the coming week.
Copper rose 100 rupees to 13,850 rupees per quintal (100 kg) in the week to Saturday and is expected to touch 14,000/14,100 rupees per quintal in the next week.
Zinc, tin and nickel were steady because of firm prices on the London Metals Exchange (LME), dealers said.
LME prices have a direct bearing on domestic prices as India imports most non-ferrous metals barring aluminium.
In cotton, arrivals continued to dwindle with most of the 1996/97 crop (October/September), estimated at 16.78 million bales of 170 kg having already been marketed, traders said.
"Prices are likely to firm further due to a shortage of quality cottons," said Mahesh Thakkar, a leading cotton trader.

Sugar prices moved higher on fears of a lower free sale quota which could create a tight supply situation, traders said. They said the quota for July was expected around 700,000 tonnes against 800,000 tonnes in the current month.
